title: Space weather and propagation prediction
blurb: Explain the radio horizon, how flares and CMEs disturb HF, and what Bz, K and A indices, VOACAP and reporting networks tell you.

E3C01.why: Flares send X-rays that arrive at light speed, causing **short-term radio blackouts**.
E3C01.trap: CMEs arrive later and drive storms, not the immediate blackout.

E3C02.why: A rising A or K index means **increasing disturbance** of the geomagnetic field.

E3C03.why: Disturbance pushes the aurora toward lower latitudes, so paths **through the auroral oval** absorb heavily.

E3C04.why: Bz is the **north-south strength** of the interplanetary magnetic field.

E3C05.why: **Southward** Bz opposes Earth's field and links up, letting charged particles disturb conditions.
E3C05.trap: Northward Bz points the same way as Earth's field and keeps things quieter.

E3C06.why: Refraction extends VHF/UHF reach, so the radio horizon is **about 15 percent farther** than the geographic one.

E3C07.why: Classes run A, B, C, M, X, each 10 times stronger. **X** is greatest.

E3C08.why: Geomagnetic storms are rated G1 to G5. **G5** is extreme.
E3C08.trap: A, B, M and X letters rate flares, not geomagnetic storms.

E3C09.why: Reporting networks collect **digital-mode and CW signals** that stations actually heard.

E3C10.why: 304 Å is **UV emission** from the Sun, and it tracks the solar flux index.

E3C11.trap: Despite the letters AC, it has nothing to do with AC power.

E3C12.why: A sudden, wide HF noise rise signals a **CME impact or a flare** has occurred.
